Published October 28, 2026 4:00 PM
More than 30 cities in L.A. and Orange counties have tax increases of some kind on the Nov. 3 ballot.
( Raymond Rivera
/
For LAist
)
Topline:
By LAist’s count, over 30 cities in Los Angeles and Orange counties are asking residents to approve tax measures on Election Day this Tuesday.
Why now? Municipalities cite stagnant revenues that haven’t kept pace with the rising costs of insurance, maintenance and infrastructure projects, and employee pensions. As a result, big cities, suburbs and small towns alike are all facing multimillion-dollar budget deficits. So they are asking residents to open their wallets — or potentially see deep cuts to basic city services.
Read on ... to find out if possible hikes are coming your way.
Full Story
Southern Californians are feeling squeezed by the rising costs of, well, everything. And now their local governments are asking for more money, too.
By LAist’s count, more than 30 cities or districts in Los Angeles and Orange counties are asking residents to approve tax measures on Election Day, Nov. 3, citing stagnant revenues that haven’t kept pace with the rising costs of insurance, maintenance and infrastructure projects, and employee pensions. Big cities, suburbs and small towns are all facing multimillion-dollar budget deficits and asking residents to open their wallets — or potentially see deep cuts to basic city services.
The list of local measures on ballots from Culver City to San Clemente includes sales taxes, hotel taxes, business taxes, parcel taxes and utility taxes. Some ballot measures would extend or increase existing taxes while others are brand-new.
Much of the answer to why so many tax measures are on the ballot lies in Proposition 13, which capped property taxes in 1978.
Before Prop. 13, cities and counties relied on property taxes for nearly all of their revenue. In the decades since, they’ve increasingly turned to other types of taxes. Hotel and utility taxes, for example, were essentially nonexistent (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497#How_Did_Proposition.A013_Change_Local_Governments_Mix_of_Tax_Revenues.3F) before the mid-1970s, and sales taxes represented a small sliver of revenue. Even as these taxes have grown, they’ve struggled to replace property tax revenue.
How Proposition 13 reshaped local taxes
Before 1978, California municipalities could raise taxes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx) without voter approval. But in addition to capping property taxes, Proposition 13 also changed the rules for other taxes. Section 4 of Proposition 13 states that any special taxes (which are taxes designated for a specific use) must be approved by two-thirds of voters. A later proposition passed in 1986 (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx) requires that general taxes be approved by a simple majority of voters. General taxes are general purpose funds that cities can allocate as they please.
The rules could change again this year with Proposition 43 (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-43-local-special-tax), which would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens to two-thirds. Currently, citizen-led special tax initiatives only need to win a simple majority.
Despite what the Nov. 3 ballot might suggest, sales tax measures are actually becoming less common, according to Michael Coleman, author of the California Local Government Finance Almanac (https://www.californiacityfinance.com/#VOTES). “More and more governments have started to exhaust the capacity for that. There’s a limit in how much you can do both legally and in terms of the tolerance of voters,” Coleman said. State law caps the maximum combined local and county sales tax rate, and many Southern California cities are already at or near that cap, Coleman said. And sales tax isn’t as reliable as it used to be, amid the broader retail downturn and shift to a service-based economy (most services aren’t taxable in California).
All of that means cities are increasingly turning to “ticky-tacky, peculiar taxes” to come up with revenue, according to Kirk Stark, a professor of tax law and policy at UCLA.
The “conventional tax instruments” — property, income and sales taxes — are all limited by state law, Stark said. “Local governments that are hoping to satisfy demand for any kind of public expenditure have to turn to other, less conventional sources of revenue.”
This year, cities are asking Southern Californians to say yes to a wide range of taxes. Below, we look at three examples in South Gate, Orange and Diamond Bar.
South Gate: A utility users tax
South Gate is asking voters to approve something less common: a utility users tax, or UUT for short. If Measure SG is approved, the 8% tax would be added to bills for utilities (https://www.cityofsouthgate.org/files/sharedassets/public/v/2/government/departments/administrative-services/budgets-amp-financial-transparency/documents/item-no.-2-uut-understanding-fiscal-challenge-presentation-4.20.26-website.pdf) such as electricity, water, natural gas, cable and phone service. The tax would bring in an estimated $10.4 million (https://www.cityofsouthgate.org/files/sharedassets/public/v/1/government/city-manager/documents/uut/sg-water-bills-insert-measure-sg.pdf) per year.
The city is facing a potential fiscal emergency and a $9.4 million budget deficit. Earlier this year, South Gate began cutting back services, including eliminating its crossing guard program and assigning fewer police officers per shift.
At a City Council meeting (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uDUbDpm7wIU&t=6192s) on the tax measure earlier this year, several residents spoke against the measure, with some calling the deficit a result of potential financial mismanagement that shouldn’t be pushed onto residents. Others said the monthly costs would simply add a new burden to already tight budgets.
“Being a homeowner here for the past 13 years, I have seen my utilities go up as well as the cost of living, my insurance for my house, and my car insurance go up. I believe there’s got to be a way to fix this problem without the UUT measure,” one resident told the City Council.
“I’m extremely frustrated that you now want to do electricity, water, sewer, cable, cell phone, gas. ... That hurts us. You’re passing that on to us, and that is absolutely not acceptable,” said another.
The only other utility users tax on the ballot in Los Angeles or Orange counties this year is in San Marino, where residents will decide whether to extend the city’s existing 5% utility users tax, which is set to expire on March 31, 2027 (https://sanmarinoca.gov/government/elections/utility_users_tax_information.php), and increase it to 6%. Last year, the tax provided almost $2.2 million (https://cms9files.revize.com/cityofsanmarino/City%20Clerk/elections/StaffReport_CONSIDERATION%20OF%20RESOLUTION%20NO.%20R-26-28.pdf?t=202607291247200) in revenue. As of 2021, a total of 162 out of 540 California cities and counties (https://californiacityfinance.com/UUTfacts21.pdf) had a utility users tax, according to Coleman’s California Local Government Finance Almanac (https://californiacityfinance.com/UUTfacts21.pdf).
Orange: Hotel and sales taxes could go up
Most people don’t book a hotel in their own city. That’s made hotel taxes an easier pill to swallow (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx) for voters, since the tax is mostly levied on visitors.
The city of Orange is asking voters to approve Measure J, which would raise the hotel tax (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/J-ORAN%20TOT%20-%20LAYOUT%20(1).pdf) from 10% to 14%. Orange is one of 10 cities across Los Angeles and Orange counties where voters will decide in November whether to increase or establish a local hotel tax, also known as a “transient occupancy tax.”
Orange residents will also vote on a 1-cent sales tax measure (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/I-ORAN%20Sales%20Tax%20-%20LAYOUT%20(1).pdf), as the city projects a $27.6 million deficit that it calls (https://www.cityoforange.org/our-city/revenue-measures) “one of the largest financial challenges in the city’s history.” The sales tax is expected to bring in $37 million annually (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/I-ORAN%20Sales%20Tax%20-%20LAYOUT%20%281%29.pdf), and the hotel tax would add $3 million (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/J-ORAN%20TOT%20-%20LAYOUT%20(1).pdf).
Diamond Bar: A new 1-cent sales tax
Diamond Bar voters will decide on Measure Q, a 1% local sales tax that would add a penny per dollar to purchases of taxable items. The city estimates the tax will bring in an additional $6 million annually, which could help plug a projected budget deficit of $5 million a year by 2030.
“The city’s challenge is simple: costs for city services are going up faster than revenues,” states Diamond Bar’s fact sheet (https://www.diamondbarca.gov/1309/Measure-Q-Preserving-Diamond-Bars-Qualit#docaccess-5e868454e42f489f95eaa188c3a27550) on the measure, which cites rising public safety costs and $100 million in infrastructure and maintenance needs.
Several other cities have local sales tax measures on the ballot, including Santa Ana’s 1.5% sales tax (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-orange-county-general-santa-ana-measure-n) extension and Los Angeles’ sales tax (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-general-los-angeles-measure-fd-sales-tax) increase for the Los Angeles Fire Department, Measure FD.
“There’s a variety because circumstances among these local governments vary. The types of economies among governments vary, the local conditions, even the preferences for what type of revenue measure or tax measure might work varies,” Coleman said. “A local government that’s looking at one of these is going to look at a number of different options and consider what might be most palatable to the voters in their community.”
What’s on your ballot?
Our LAist Voter Game Plan is here to help guide you through the Nov. 3 election with guides to races across Los Angeles and Orange counties — and that long list of state propositions — to help you cast a ballot that’s in line with your own personal beliefs and values.
But the one thing we don’t do? We don’t tell you how to vote. That part is left up to you.
You can find it all at LAist.com/Vote (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides).

Topline:
L.A. County quietly stopped handing out syringes and pipes at its Skid Row Care Campus in August and has ended its contract with Homeless Health Care Los Angeles, the nonprofit that ran harm reduction there, effective Tuesday.
Why it matters : The goal of these programs is to keep people who use drugs alive and free of infections like HIV and hepatitis, while working to connect them with services including treatment. The pause comes amid a growing cluster of HIV cases in Skid Row.
Why now: The county says the temporary pause stems “in part” from concerns raised by community stakeholders and local businesses.
What’s next: Homeless Health Care Los Angeles is laying off 134 workers. New providers have rehired many of them, the county says.

Proposition 43
Raise vote threshold for special tax measures
This would make it harder to impose or increase local taxes by raising the threshold for local citizen-driven special tax ballot initiatives to pass from a simple majority to two-thirds. The two-thirds threshold already applies to taxes proposed by local governments but not by individuals. The measure reflects a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Raise vote threshold for special tax measures
This would make it harder to impose or increase local taxes by raising the threshold for local citizen-driven special tax ballot initiatives to pass from a simple majority to two-thirds. More than 30 cities in L.A. and Orange counties have tax increases of some kind on the Nov. 3 ballot.
( Raymond Rivera
/
For LAist
)
Topline:
By LAist’s count, over 30 cities in Los Angeles and Orange counties are asking residents to approve tax measures on Election Day this Tuesday.
Why now? Municipalities cite stagnant revenues that haven’t kept pace with the rising costs of insurance, maintenance and infrastructure projects, and employee pensions. As a result, big cities, suburbs and small towns alike are all facing multimillion-dollar budget deficits. So they are asking residents to open their wallets — or potentially see deep cuts to basic city services.
Read on ... to find out if possible hikes are coming your way.
Full Story
Southern Californians are feeling squeezed by the rising costs of, well, everything. And now their local governments are asking for more money, too.
By LAist’s count, more than 30 cities or districts in Los Angeles and Orange counties are asking residents to approve tax measures on Election Day, Nov. 3, citing stagnant revenues that haven’t kept pace with the rising costs of insurance, maintenance and infrastructure projects, and employee pensions. Big cities, suburbs and small towns are all facing multimillion-dollar budget deficits and asking residents to open their wallets — or potentially see deep cuts to basic city services.
The list of local measures on ballots from Culver City to San Clemente includes sales taxes, hotel taxes, business taxes, parcel taxes and utility taxes. Some ballot measures would extend or increase existing taxes while others are brand-new.
Much of the answer to why so many tax measures are on the ballot lies in Proposition 13, which capped property taxes in 1978.
Before Prop. 13, cities and counties relied on property taxes for nearly all of their revenue. In the decades since, they’ve increasingly turned to other types of taxes. Hotel and utility taxes, for example, were essentially nonexistent (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497#How_Did_Proposition.A013_Change_Local_Governments_Mix_of_Tax_Revenues.3F) before the mid-1970s, and sales taxes represented a small sliver of revenue. Even as these taxes have grown, they’ve struggled to replace property tax revenue.
How Proposition 13 reshaped local taxes
Before 1978, California municipalities could raise taxes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx) without voter approval. But in addition to capping property taxes, Proposition 13 also changed the rules for other taxes. Section 4 of Proposition 13 states that any special taxes (which are taxes designated for a specific use) must be approved by two-thirds of voters. A later proposition passed in 1986 (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx) requires that general taxes be approved by a simple majority of voters. General taxes are general purpose funds that cities can allocate as they please.
The rules could change again this year with Proposition 43 (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-43-local-special-tax), which would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens to two-thirds. Currently, citizen-led special tax initiatives only need to win a simple majority.
Despite what the Nov. 3 ballot might suggest, sales tax measures are actually becoming less common, according to Michael Coleman, author of the California Local Government Finance Almanac (https://www.californiacityfinance.com/#VOTES). “More and more governments have started to exhaust the capacity for that. There’s a limit in how much you can do both legally and in terms of the tolerance of voters,” Coleman said. State law caps the maximum combined local and county sales tax rate, and many Southern California cities are already at or near that cap, Coleman said. And sales tax isn’t as reliable as it used to be, amid the broader retail downturn and shift to a service-based economy (most services aren’t taxable in California).
All of that means cities are increasingly turning to “ticky-tacky, peculiar taxes” to come up with revenue, according to Kirk Stark, a professor of tax law and policy at UCLA.
The “conventional tax instruments” — property, income and sales taxes — are all limited by state law, Stark said. “Local governments that are hoping to satisfy demand for any kind of public expenditure have to turn to other, less conventional sources of revenue.”
This year, cities are asking Southern Californians to say yes to a wide range of taxes. Below, we look at three examples in South Gate, Orange and Diamond Bar.
South Gate: A utility users tax
South Gate is asking voters to approve something less common: a utility users tax, or UUT for short. If Measure SG is approved, the 8% tax would be added to bills for utilities (https://www.cityofsouthgate.org/files/sharedassets/public/v/2/government/departments/administrative-services/budgets-amp-financial-transparency/documents/item-no.-2-uut-understanding-fiscal-challenge-presentation-4.20.26-website.pdf) such as electricity, water, natural gas, cable and phone service. The tax would bring in an estimated $10.4 million (https://www.cityofsouthgate.org/files/sharedassets/public/v/1/government/city-manager/documents/uut/sg-water-bills-insert-measure-sg.pdf) per year.
The city is facing a potential fiscal emergency and a $9.4 million budget deficit. Earlier this year, South Gate began cutting back services, including eliminating its crossing guard program and assigning fewer police officers per shift.
At a City Council meeting (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uDUbDpm7wIU&t=6192s) on the tax measure earlier this year, several residents spoke against the measure, with some calling the deficit a result of potential financial mismanagement that shouldn’t be pushed onto residents. Others said the monthly costs would simply add a new burden to already tight budgets.
“Being a homeowner here for the past 13 years, I have seen my utilities go up as well as the cost of living, my insurance for my house, and my car insurance go up. I believe there’s got to be a way to fix this problem without the UUT measure,” one resident told the City Council.
“I’m extremely frustrated that you now want to do electricity, water, sewer, cable, cell phone, gas. ... That hurts us. You’re passing that on to us, and that is absolutely not acceptable,” said another.
The only other utility users tax on the ballot in Los Angeles or Orange counties this year is in San Marino, where residents will decide whether to extend the city’s existing 5% utility users tax, which is set to expire on March 31, 2027 (https://sanmarinoca.gov/government/elections/utility_users_tax_information.php), and increase it to 6%. Last year, the tax provided almost $2.2 million (https://cms9files.revize.com/cityofsanmarino/City%20Clerk/elections/StaffReport_CONSIDERATION%20OF%20RESOLUTION%20NO.%20R-26-28.pdf?t=202607291247200) in revenue. As of 2021, a total of 162 out of 540 California cities and counties (https://californiacityfinance.com/UUTfacts21.pdf) had a utility users tax, according to Coleman’s California Local Government Finance Almanac (https://californiacityfinance.com/UUTfacts21.pdf).
Orange: Hotel and sales taxes could go up
Most people don’t book a hotel in their own city. That’s made hotel taxes an easier pill to swallow (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx) for voters, since the tax is mostly levied on visitors.
The city of Orange is asking voters to approve Measure J, which would raise the hotel tax (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/J-ORAN%20TOT%20-%20LAYOUT%20(1).pdf) from 10% to 14%. Orange is one of 10 cities across Los Angeles and Orange counties where voters will decide in November whether to increase or establish a local hotel tax, also known as a “transient occupancy tax.”
Orange residents will also vote on a 1-cent sales tax measure (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/I-ORAN%20Sales%20Tax%20-%20LAYOUT%20(1).pdf), as the city projects a $27.6 million deficit that it calls (https://www.cityoforange.org/our-city/revenue-measures) “one of the largest financial challenges in the city’s history.” The sales tax is expected to bring in $37 million annually (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/I-ORAN%20Sales%20Tax%20-%20LAYOUT%20%281%29.pdf), and the hotel tax would add $3 million (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/J-ORAN%20TOT%20-%20LAYOUT%20(1).pdf).
Diamond Bar: A new 1-cent sales tax
Diamond Bar voters will decide on Measure Q, a 1% local sales tax that would add a penny per dollar to purchases of taxable items. The city estimates the tax will bring in an additional $6 million annually, which could help plug a projected budget deficit of $5 million a year by 2030.
“The city’s challenge is simple: costs for city services are going up faster than revenues,” states Diamond Bar’s fact sheet (https://www.diamondbarca.gov/1309/Measure-Q-Preserving-Diamond-Bars-Qualit#docaccess-5e868454e42f489f95eaa188c3a27550) on the measure, which cites rising public safety costs and $100 million in infrastructure and maintenance needs.
Several other cities have local sales tax measures on the ballot, including Santa Ana’s 1.5% sales tax (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-orange-county-general-santa-ana-measure-n) extension and Los Angeles’ sales tax (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-general-los-angeles-measure-fd-sales-tax) increase for the Los Angeles Fire Department, Measure FD.
“There’s a variety because circumstances among these local governments vary. The types of economies among governments vary, the local conditions, even the preferences for what type of revenue measure or tax measure might work varies,” Coleman said. “A local government that’s looking at one of these is going to look at a number of different options and consider what might be most palatable to the voters in their community.”
What’s on your ballot?
Our LAist Voter Game Plan is here to help guide you through the Nov. 3 election with guides to races across Los Angeles and Orange counties — and that long list of state propositions — to help you cast a ballot that’s in line with your own personal beliefs and values.
But the one thing we don’t do? We don’t tell you how to vote. That part is left up to you.

All the tax measures on the LA, OC ballots
Erin Rode (https://laist.com/people/erin-rode)
is working on election coverage this fall, along with other topics.
Published October 28, 2026 4:00 PM
More than 30 cities in L.A. and Orange counties have tax increases of some kind on the Nov. 3 ballot.
( Raymond Rivera
/
For LAist
)
Topline:
By LAist’s count, over 30 cities in Los Angeles and Orange counties are asking residents to approve tax measures on Election Day this Tuesday.
Why now? Municipalities cite stagnant revenues that haven’t kept pace with the rising costs of insurance, maintenance and infrastructure projects, and employee pensions. As a result, big cities, suburbs and small towns alike are all facing multimillion-dollar budget deficits. So they are asking residents to open their wallets — or potentially see deep cuts to basic city services.
Read on ... to find out if possible hikes are coming your way.
Full Story
Southern Californians are feeling squeezed by the rising costs of, well, everything. And now their local governments are asking for more money, too.
By LAist’s count, more than 30 cities or districts in Los Angeles and Orange counties are asking residents to approve tax measures on Election Day, Nov. 3, citing stagnant revenues that haven’t kept pace with the rising costs of insurance, maintenance and infrastructure projects, and employee pensions. Big cities, suburbs and small towns are all facing multimillion-dollar budget deficits and asking residents to open their wallets — or potentially see deep cuts to basic city services.
The list of local measures on ballots from Culver City to San Clemente includes sales taxes, hotel taxes, business taxes, parcel taxes and utility taxes. Some ballot measures would extend or increase existing taxes while others are brand-new.
Much of the answer to why so many tax measures are on the ballot lies in Proposition 13, which capped property taxes in 1978.
Before Prop. 13, cities and counties relied on property taxes for nearly all of their revenue. In the decades since, they’ve increasingly turned to other types of taxes. Hotel and utility taxes, for example, were essentially nonexistent (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497#How_Did_Proposition.A013_Change_Local_Governments_Mix_of_Tax_Revenues.3F) before the mid-1970s, and sales taxes represented a small sliver of revenue. Even as these taxes have grown, they’ve struggled to replace property tax revenue.
How Proposition 13 reshaped local taxes
Before 1978, California municipalities could raise taxes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx) without voter approval. But in addition to capping property taxes, Proposition 13 also changed the rules for other taxes. Section 4 of Proposition 13 states that any special taxes (which are taxes designated for a specific use) must be approved by two-thirds of voters. A later proposition passed in 1986 (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx) requires that general taxes be approved by a simple majority of voters. General taxes are general purpose funds that cities can allocate as they please.
The rules could change again this year with Proposition 43 (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-43-local-special-tax), which would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens to two-thirds. Currently, citizen-led special tax initiatives only need to win a simple majority.
Despite what the Nov. 3 ballot might suggest, sales tax measures are actually becoming less common, according to Michael Coleman, author of the California Local Government Finance Almanac (https://www.californiacityfinance.com/#VOTES). “More and more governments have started to exhaust the capacity for that. There’s a limit in how much you can do both legally and in terms of the tolerance of voters,” Coleman said. State law caps the maximum combined local and county sales tax rate, and many Southern California cities are already at or near that cap, Coleman said. And sales tax isn’t as reliable as it used to be, amid the broader retail downturn and shift to a service-based economy (most services aren’t taxable in California).
All of that means cities are increasingly turning to “ticky-tacky, peculiar taxes” to come up with revenue, according to Kirk Stark, a professor of tax law and policy at UCLA.
The “conventional tax instruments” — property, income and sales taxes — are all limited by state law, Stark said. “Local governments that are hoping to satisfy demand for any kind of public expenditure have to turn to other, less conventional sources of revenue.”
This year, cities are asking Southern Californians to say yes to a wide range of taxes. Below, we look at three examples in South Gate, Orange and Diamond Bar.
South Gate: A utility users tax
South Gate is asking voters to approve something less common: a utility users tax, or UUT for short. If Measure SG is approved, the 8% tax would be added to bills for utilities (https://www.cityofsouthgate.org/files/sharedassets/public/v/2/government/departments/administrative-services/budgets-amp-financial-transparency/documents/item-no.-2-uut-understanding-fiscal-challenge-presentation-4.20.26-website.pdf) such as electricity, water, natural gas, cable and phone service. The tax would bring in an estimated $10.4 million (https://www.cityofsouthgate.org/files/sharedassets/public/v/1/government/city-manager/documents/uut/sg-water-bills-insert-measure-sg.pdf) per year.
The city is facing a potential fiscal emergency and a $9.4 million budget deficit. Earlier this year, South Gate began cutting back services, including eliminating its crossing guard program and assigning fewer police officers per shift.
At a City Council meeting (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uDUbDpm7wIU&t=6192s) on the tax measure earlier this year, several residents spoke against the measure, with some calling the deficit a result of potential financial mismanagement that shouldn’t be pushed onto residents. Others said the monthly costs would simply add a new burden to already tight budgets.
“Being a homeowner here for the past 13 years, I have seen my utilities go up as well as the cost of living, my insurance for my house, and my car insurance go up. I believe there’s got to be a way to fix this problem without the UUT measure,” one resident told the City Council.
“I’m extremely frustrated that you now want to do electricity, water, sewer, cable, cell phone, gas. ... That hurts us. You’re passing that on to us, and that is absolutely not acceptable,” said another.
The only other utility users tax on the ballot in Los Angeles or Orange counties this year is in San Marino, where residents will decide whether to extend the city’s existing 5% utility users tax, which is set to expire on March 31, 2027 (https://sanmarinoca.gov/government/elections/utility_users_tax_information.php), and increase it to 6%. Last year, the tax provided almost $2.2 million (https://cms9files.revize.com/cityofsanmarino/City%20Clerk/elections/StaffReport_CONSIDERATION%20OF%20RESOLUTION%20NO.%20R-26-28.pdf?t=202607291247200) in revenue. As of 2021, a total of 162 out of 540 California cities and counties (https://californiacityfinance.com/UUTfacts21.pdf) had a utility users tax, according to Coleman’s California Local Government Finance Almanac (https://californiacityfinance.com/UUTfacts21.pdf).
Orange: Hotel and sales taxes could go up
Most people don’t book a hotel in their own city. That’s made hotel taxes an easier pill to swallow (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx) for voters, since the tax is mostly levied on visitors.
The city of Orange is asking voters to approve Measure J, which would raise the hotel tax (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/J-ORAN%20TOT%20-%20LAYOUT%20(1).pdf) from 10% to 14%. Orange is one of 10 cities across Los Angeles and Orange counties where voters will decide in November whether to increase or establish a local hotel tax, also known as a “transient occupancy tax.”
Orange residents will also vote on a 1-cent sales tax measure (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/I-ORAN%20Sales%20Tax%20-%20LAYOUT%20(1).pdf), as the city projects a $27.6 million deficit that it calls (https://www.cityoforange.org/our-city/revenue-measures) “one of the largest financial challenges in the city’s history.” The sales tax is expected to bring in $37 million annually (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/I-ORAN%20Sales%20Tax%20-%20LAYOUT%20%281%29.pdf), and the hotel tax would add $3 million (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/J-ORAN%20TOT%20-%20LAYOUT%20(1).pdf).
Diamond Bar: A new 1-cent sales tax
Diamond Bar voters will decide on Measure Q, a 1% local sales tax that would add a penny per dollar to purchases of taxable items. The city estimates the tax will bring in an additional $6 million annually, which could help plug a projected budget deficit of $5 million a year by 2030.
“The city’s challenge is simple: costs for city services are going up faster than revenues,” states Diamond Bar’s fact sheet (https://www.diamondbarca.gov/1309/Measure-Q-Preserving-Diamond-Bars-Qualit#docaccess-5e868454e42f489f95eaa188c3a27550) on the measure, which cites rising public safety costs and $100 million in infrastructure and maintenance needs.
Several other cities have local sales tax measures on the ballot, including Santa Ana’s 1.5% sales tax (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-orange-county-general-santa-ana-measure-n) extension and Los Angeles’ sales tax (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-general-los-angeles-measure-fd-sales-tax) increase for the Los Angeles Fire Department, Measure FD.
“There’s a variety because circumstances among these local governments vary. The types of economies among governments vary, the local conditions, even the preferences for what type of revenue measure or tax measure might work varies,” Coleman said. “A local government that’s looking at one of these is going to look at a number of different options and consider what might be most palatable to the voters in their community.”
What’s on your ballot?
Our LAist Voter Game Plan is here to help guide you through the Nov. 3 election with guides to races across Los Angeles and Orange counties — and that long list of state propositions — to help you cast a ballot that’s in line with your own personal beliefs and values.
But the one thing we don’t do? We don’t tell you how to vote. That part is left up to you.
You can find it all at LAist.com/Vote (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides).

Proposition 43
Raise vote threshold for special tax measures
This would make it harder to impose or increase local taxes by raising the threshold for local citizen-driven special tax ballot initiatives to pass from a simple majority to two-thirds. The two-thirds threshold already applies to taxes proposed by local governments but not by individuals. The measure reflects a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. Published October 28, 2026 4:00 PM
More than 30 cities in L.A. and Orange counties have tax increases of some kind on the Nov. 3 ballot.
( Raymond Rivera
/
For LAist
)
Topline:
By LAist’s count, over 30 cities in Los Angeles and Orange counties are asking residents to approve tax measures on Election Day this Tuesday.
Why now? Municipalities cite stagnant revenues that haven’t kept pace with the rising costs of insurance, maintenance and infrastructure projects, and employee pensions. As a result, big cities, suburbs and small towns alike are all facing multimillion-dollar budget deficits. So they are asking residents to open their wallets — or potentially see deep cuts to basic city services.
Read on ... to find out if possible hikes are coming your way.
Full Story
Southern Californians are feeling squeezed by the rising costs of, well, everything. And now their local governments are asking for more money, too.
By LAist’s count, more than 30 cities or districts in Los Angeles and Orange counties are asking residents to approve tax measures on Election Day, Nov. 3, citing stagnant revenues that haven’t kept pace with the rising costs of insurance, maintenance and infrastructure projects, and employee pensions. Big cities, suburbs and small towns are all facing multimillion-dollar budget deficits and asking residents to open their wallets — or potentially see deep cuts to basic city services.
The list of local measures on ballots from Culver City to San Clemente includes sales taxes, hotel taxes, business taxes, parcel taxes and utility taxes. Some ballot measures would extend or increase existing taxes while others are brand-new.
Much of the answer to why so many tax measures are on the ballot lies in Proposition 13, which capped property taxes in 1978.
Before Prop. 13, cities and counties relied on property taxes for nearly all of their revenue. In the decades since, they’ve increasingly turned to other types of taxes. Hotel and utility taxes, for example, were essentially nonexistent (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497#How_Did_Proposition.A013_Change_Local_Governments_Mix_of_Tax_Revenues.3F) before the mid-1970s, and sales taxes represented a small sliver of revenue. Even as these taxes have grown, they’ve struggled to replace property tax revenue.
How Proposition 13 reshaped local taxes
Before 1978, California municipalities could raise taxes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx) without voter approval. But in addition to capping property taxes, Proposition 13 also changed the rules for other taxes. Section 4 of Proposition 13 states that any special taxes (which are taxes designated for a specific use) must be approved by two-thirds of voters. A later proposition passed in 1986 (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx) requires that general taxes be approved by a simple majority of voters. General taxes are general purpose funds that cities can allocate as they please.
The rules could change again this year with Proposition 43 (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-43-local-special-tax), which would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens to two-thirds. Currently, citizen-led special tax initiatives only need to win a simple majority.
Despite what the Nov. 3 ballot might suggest, sales tax measures are actually becoming less common, according to Michael Coleman, author of the California Local Government Finance Almanac (https://www.californiacityfinance.com/#VOTES). “More and more governments have started to exhaust the capacity for that. There’s a limit in how much you can do both legally and in terms of the tolerance of voters,” Coleman said. State law caps the maximum combined local and county sales tax rate, and many Southern California cities are already at or near that cap, Coleman said. And sales tax isn’t as reliable as it used to be, amid the broader retail downturn and shift to a service-based economy (most services aren’t taxable in California).
All of that means cities are increasingly turning to “ticky-tacky, peculiar taxes” to come up with revenue, according to Kirk Stark, a professor of tax law and policy at UCLA.
The “conventional tax instruments” — property, income and sales taxes — are all limited by state law, Stark said. “Local governments that are hoping to satisfy demand for any kind of public expenditure have to turn to other, less conventional sources of revenue.”
This year, cities are asking Southern Californians to say yes to a wide range of taxes. Below, we look at three examples in South Gate, Orange and Diamond Bar.
South Gate: A utility users tax
South Gate is asking voters to approve something less common: a utility users tax, or UUT for short. If Measure SG is approved, the 8% tax would be added to bills for utilities (https://www.cityofsouthgate.org/files/sharedassets/public/v/2/government/departments/administrative-services/budgets-amp-financial-transparency/documents/item-no.-2-uut-understanding-fiscal-challenge-presentation-4.20.26-website.pdf) such as electricity, water, natural gas, cable and phone service. The tax would bring in an estimated $10.4 million (https://www.cityofsouthgate.org/files/sharedassets/public/v/1/government/city-manager/documents/uut/sg-water-bills-insert-measure-sg.pdf) per year.
The city is facing a potential fiscal emergency and a $9.4 million budget deficit. Earlier this year, South Gate began cutting back services, including eliminating its crossing guard program and assigning fewer police officers per shift.
At a City Council meeting (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uDUbDpm7wIU&t=6192s) on the tax measure earlier this year, several residents spoke against the measure, with some calling the deficit a result of potential financial mismanagement that shouldn’t be pushed onto residents. Others said the monthly costs would simply add a new burden to already tight budgets.
“Being a homeowner here for the past 13 years, I have seen my utilities go up as well as the cost of living, my insurance for my house, and my car insurance go up. I believe there’s got to be a way to fix this problem without the UUT measure,” one resident told the City Council.
“I’m extremely frustrated that you now want to do electricity, water, sewer, cable, cell phone, gas. ... That hurts us. You’re passing that on to us, and that is absolutely not acceptable,” said another.
The only other utility users tax on the ballot in Los Angeles or Orange counties this year is in San Marino, where residents will decide whether to extend the city’s existing 5% utility users tax, which is set to expire on March 31, 2027 (https://sanmarinoca.gov/government/elections/utility_users_tax_information.php), and increase it to 6%. Last year, the tax provided almost $2.2 million (https://cms9files.revize.com/cityofsanmarino/City%20Clerk/elections/StaffReport_CONSIDERATION%20OF%20RESOLUTION%20NO.%20R-26-28.pdf?t=202607291247200) in revenue. As of 2021, a total of 162 out of 540 California cities and counties (https://californiacityfinance.com/UUTfacts21.pdf) had a utility users tax, according to Coleman’s California Local Government Finance Almanac (https://californiacityfinance.com/UUTfacts21.pdf).
Orange: Hotel and sales taxes could go up
Most people don’t book a hotel in their own city. That’s made hotel taxes an easier pill to swallow (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx) for voters, since the tax is mostly levied on visitors.
The city of Orange is asking voters to approve Measure J, which would raise the hotel tax (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/J-ORAN%20TOT%20-%20LAYOUT%20(1).pdf) from 10% to 14%. Orange is one of 10 cities across Los Angeles and Orange counties where voters will decide in November whether to increase or establish a local hotel tax, also known as a “transient occupancy tax.”
Orange residents will also vote on a 1-cent sales tax measure (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/I-ORAN%20Sales%20Tax%20-%20LAYOUT%20(1).pdf), as the city projects a $27.6 million deficit that it calls (https://www.cityoforange.org/our-city/revenue-measures) “one of the largest financial challenges in the city’s history.” The sales tax is expected to bring in $37 million annually (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/I-ORAN%20Sales%20Tax%20-%20LAYOUT%20%281%29.pdf), and the hotel tax would add $3 million (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/J-ORAN%20TOT%20-%20LAYOUT%20(1).pdf).
Diamond Bar: A new 1-cent sales tax
Diamond Bar voters will decide on Measure Q, a 1% local sales tax that would add a penny per dollar to purchases of taxable items. The city estimates the tax will bring in an additional $6 million annually, which could help plug a projected budget deficit of $5 million a year by 2030.
“The city’s challenge is simple: costs for city services are going up faster than revenues,” states Diamond Bar’s fact sheet (https://www.diamondbarca.gov/1309/Measure-Q-Preserving-Diamond-Bars-Qualit#docaccess-5e868454e42f489f95eaa188c3a27550) on the measure, which cites rising public safety costs and $100 million in infrastructure and maintenance needs.
Several other cities have local sales tax measures on the ballot, including Santa Ana’s 1.5% sales tax (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-orange-county-general-santa-ana-measure-n) extension and Los Angeles’ sales tax (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-general-los-angeles-measure-fd-sales-tax) increase for the Los Angeles Fire Department, Measure FD.
“There’s a variety because circumstances among these local governments vary. The types of economies among governments vary, the local conditions, even the preferences for what type of revenue measure or tax measure might work varies,” Coleman said. “A local government that’s looking at one of these is going to look at a number of different options and consider what might be most palatable to the voters in their community.”
What’s on your ballot?
Our LAist Voter Game Plan is here to help guide you through the Nov. 3 election with guides to races across Los Angeles and Orange counties — and that long list of state propositions — to help you cast a ballot that’s in line with your own personal beliefs and values.
But the one thing we don’t do? We don’t tell you how to vote. That part is left up to you.
You can find it all at LAist.com/Vote (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides).

Topline:
L.A. County quietly stopped handing out syringes and pipes at its Skid Row Care Campus in August and has ended its contract with Homeless Health Care Los Angeles, the nonprofit that ran harm reduction there, effective Tuesday.
Why it matters : The goal of these programs is to keep people who use drugs alive and free of infections like HIV and hepatitis, while working to connect them with services including treatment. The pause comes amid a growing cluster of HIV cases in Skid Row.

Learn more here (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/). California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, an anti-tax advocate says Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied. The opposing view: A city councilmember from Sonoma believes Prop. 43 enables minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/), making it harder to fund vital government functions . Guest Commentary written by Susan Shelley Susan Shelley is the vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The November ballot measure Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) would make it harder to raise taxes in California by restoring the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. A “special tax” is one that earmarks the revenue for specific purposes. Ever since voters approved Proposition 13 in 1978 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)), the California Constitution has clearly stated that cities, counties and special districts may impose special taxes “by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district.” If courts had enforced that plain language, Californians today would not be paying billions of dollars in local taxes. This includes sales tax increases such as L.A. County’s 2024 Measure A (https://homeless.lacounty.gov/measure-a/) for homelessness programs, as well as Measure ULA in the city of Los Angeles (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/), a real estate transfer tax on the value of a property worth more than $5 million, which also pays for homelessness programs and affordable housing. Neither of these received the constitutionally required 66.67% of the vote. In San Francisco, courts upheld a June 2018 special tax (http://sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-appeals-court-upholds-S-F-s-commercial-15903302.php) on commercial real estate leases to fund early education and child care, and a November 2018 special tax on the gross receipts of businesses to pay for homelessness programs. Just like Los Angeles, these measures fell short of a two-thirds vote. In 1978, the people of California added the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes to their constitution. When did the constitution become merely advisory? READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/) It began in 2017 with ambiguous language in a California Supreme Court decision, California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (https://cases.justia.com/california/supreme-court/2017-s234148.pdf?ts=1503939675) . The court suggested — without really deciding — that if a tax increase was placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative instead of by a city council or other government body, the constitution didn’t necessarily apply, and a two-thirds vote wasn’t necessarily required. Lower courts used that language to uphold special taxes that received less than a two-thirds vote if they were placed on the ballot by voters signing initiative petitions. But who are these citizens who want to stand outside grocery stores and farmer’s markets with clipboards to raise their own taxes? They’re often the people who will get the money from the tax. The Upland decision has essentially enabled special interest groups (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) to write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves, pay to collect the signatures to get it on the ballot, and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Some of the court rulings on these Upland taxes have even allowed local government officials to work hand-in-glove with special interests (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/the-fiction-of-citizens-tax-initiatives-in-california/) to get tax increases on the ballot as “citizens’ initiatives.” Now the state government is pushing the envelope even further. The governor recently signed Assembly Bill 1923 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1923), requiring the Fresno County Registrar of Voters to place a citizens’ initiative sales tax increase for transportation on the November ballot (https://fresnoland.org/2026/08/06/better-roads/). The state did this over the objections of the Fresno County Board of Supervisors after it lawfully exercised its discretion under the elections code to order a study of the measure, which would have delayed it past the 2026 ballot deadline and placed it on the 2028 ballot. This is no way to run a railroad. There is no “citizens’ initiative tax increase exception” from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up. Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes. Prop. 43 will restore the two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including any tax increases placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative. It’s a constitutional amendment, overriding court precedents that say otherwise. General taxes, such as those that direct the revenue into a city or county general fund to be spent as elected officials decide, would continue to require only a simple majority vote. Some local government officials may believe voters will not approve general taxes, so they would prefer to tell voters the money from a new tax will be spent only on a specific, urgent need. Their problem isn’t the constitution, it’s trust — if voters don’t trust local elected officials to spend tax money on the most important priorities first, a majority may vote ‘no’ on any tax unless they know what it will fund and it’s guaranteed in writing. Those same officials undoubtedly benefit from having a court-created loophole to raise special taxes without the need for a two-thirds vote. The loophole has been growing with every election. Multiple “citizens’ initiative” tax increases are on the November ballot, racing to squeeze through the opening before voters can hammer boards over it. Prop. 43 gives California voters the opportunity to restore what state courts have eroded: a taxpayer protection in the state constitution that requires local special taxes to have the approval of two-thirds of voters to pass. Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments

By Sandra Lowe, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, a city councilmember from Sonoma believes Proposition 43 enables minority rule, making it harder to fund vital government functions. The opposing view: An anti-tax advocate says Prop. 43 solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied.

Guest Commentary written by

Sometimes things that sound simple are not. 

Let’s take Proposition 43. Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments' decisions: majority rule.  

Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority.

Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected.

In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee.

Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. 

If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote.

The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders.

No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent.

Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions.

The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation.  

Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime.

Majority rule is the basis of our democracy and a hallmark of a free society. Let's not go backward.

Guest Commentary written by Susan Shelley Susan Shelley is the vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The November ballot measure Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) would make it harder to raise taxes in California by restoring the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. A “special tax” is one that earmarks the revenue for specific purposes. Ever since voters approved Proposition 13 in 1978 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)), the California Constitution has clearly stated that cities, counties and special districts may impose special taxes “by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district.” If courts had enforced that plain language, Californians today would not be paying billions of dollars in local taxes. This includes sales tax increases such as L.A. County’s 2024 Measure A (https://homeless.lacounty.gov/measure-a/) for homelessness programs, as well as Measure ULA in the city of Los Angeles (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/), a real estate transfer tax on the value of a property worth more than $5 million, which also pays for homelessness programs and affordable housing. Neither of these received the constitutionally required 66.67% of the vote. In San Francisco, courts upheld a June 2018 special tax (http://sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-appeals-court-upholds-S-F-s-commercial-15903302.php) on commercial real estate leases to fund early education and child care, and a November 2018 special tax on the gross receipts of businesses to pay for homelessness programs. Just like Los Angeles, these measures fell short of a two-thirds vote. In 1978, the people of California added the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes to their constitution. When did the constitution become merely advisory? READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/) It began in 2017 with ambiguous language in a California Supreme Court decision, California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (https://cases.justia.com/california/supreme-court/2017-s234148.pdf?ts=1503939675) . The court suggested — without really deciding — that if a tax increase was placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative instead of by a city council or other government body, the constitution didn’t necessarily apply, and a two-thirds vote wasn’t necessarily required. Lower courts used that language to uphold special taxes that received less than a two-thirds vote if they were placed on the ballot by voters signing initiative petitions. But who are these citizens who want to stand outside grocery stores and farmer’s markets with clipboards to raise their own taxes? They’re often the people who will get the money from the tax. The Upland decision has essentially enabled special interest groups (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) to write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves, pay to collect the signatures to get it on the ballot, and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Some of the court rulings on these Upland taxes have even allowed local government officials to work hand-in-glove with special interests (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/the-fiction-of-citizens-tax-initiatives-in-california/) to get tax increases on the ballot as “citizens’ initiatives.” Now the state government is pushing the envelope even further. The governor recently signed Assembly Bill 1923 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1923), requiring the Fresno County Registrar of Voters to place a citizens’ initiative sales tax increase for transportation on the November ballot (https://fresnoland.org/2026/08/06/better-roads/). The state did this over the objections of the Fresno County Board of Supervisors after it lawfully exercised its discretion under the elections code to order a study of the measure, which would have delayed it past the 2026 ballot deadline and placed it on the 2028 ballot. This is no way to run a railroad. There is no “citizens’ initiative tax increase exception” from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up. Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes. Prop. 43 will restore the two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including any tax increases placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative. It’s a constitutional amendment, overriding court precedents that say otherwise. General taxes, such as those that direct the revenue into a city or county general fund to be spent as elected officials decide, would continue to require only a simple majority vote. Some local government officials may believe voters will not approve general taxes, so they would prefer to tell voters the money from a new tax will be spent only on a specific, urgent need. Their problem isn’t the constitution, it’s trust — if voters don’t trust local elected officials to spend tax money on the most important priorities first, a majority may vote ‘no’ on any tax unless they know what it will fund and it’s guaranteed in writing. Those same officials undoubtedly benefit from having a court-created loophole to raise special taxes without the need for a two-thirds vote. The loophole has been growing with every election. Multiple “citizens’ initiative” tax increases are on the November ballot, racing to squeeze through the opening before voters can hammer boards over it. Prop. 43 gives California voters the opportunity to restore what state courts have eroded: a taxpayer protection in the state constitution that requires local special taxes to have the approval of two-thirds of voters to pass. Below, an anti-tax advocate says Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied. The opposing view: A city councilmember from Sonoma believes Prop. 43 enables minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/), making it harder to fund vital government functions . Guest Commentary written by Susan Shelley Susan Shelley is the vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The November ballot measure Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) would make it harder to raise taxes in California by restoring the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. A “special tax” is one that earmarks the revenue for specific purposes. Ever since voters approved Proposition 13 in 1978 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)), the California Constitution has clearly stated that cities, counties and special districts may impose special taxes “by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district.” If courts had enforced that plain language, Californians today would not be paying billions of dollars in local taxes. This includes sales tax increases such as L.A. County’s 2024 Measure A (https://homeless.lacounty.gov/measure-a/) for homelessness programs, as well as Measure ULA in the city of Los Angeles (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/), a real estate transfer tax on the value of a property worth more than $5 million, which also pays for homelessness programs and affordable housing. Neither of these received the constitutionally required 66.67% of the vote. In San Francisco, courts upheld a June 2018 special tax (http://sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-appeals-court-upholds-S-F-s-commercial-15903302.php) on commercial real estate leases to fund early education and child care, and a November 2018 special tax on the gross receipts of businesses to pay for homelessness programs. Just like Los Angeles, these measures fell short of a two-thirds vote. In 1978, the people of California added the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes to their constitution. When did the constitution become merely advisory? READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/) It began in 2017 with ambiguous language in a California Supreme Court decision, California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (https://cases.justia.com/california/supreme-court/2017-s234148.pdf?ts=1503939675) . The court suggested — without really deciding — that if a tax increase was placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative instead of by a city council or other government body, the constitution didn’t necessarily apply, and a two-thirds vote wasn’t necessarily required. Lower courts used that language to uphold special taxes that received less than a two-thirds vote if they were placed on the ballot by voters signing initiative petitions. But who are these citizens who want to stand outside grocery stores and farmer’s markets with clipboards to raise their own taxes? They’re often the people who will get the money from the tax. The Upland decision has essentially enabled special interest groups (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) to write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves, pay to collect the signatures to get it on the ballot, and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Some of the court rulings on these Upland taxes have even allowed local government officials to work hand-in-glove with special interests (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/the-fiction-of-citizens-tax-initiatives-in-california/) to get tax increases on the ballot as “citizens’ initiatives.” Now the state government is pushing the envelope even further. The governor recently signed Assembly Bill 1923 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1923), requiring the Fresno County Registrar of Voters to place a citizens’ initiative sales tax increase for transportation on the November ballot (https://fresnoland.org/2026/08/06/better-roads/). The state did this over the objections of the Fresno County Board of Supervisors after it lawfully exercised its discretion under the elections code to order a study of the measure, which would have delayed it past the 2026 ballot deadline and placed it on the 2028 ballot. This is no way to run a railroad. There is no “citizens’ initiative tax increase exception” from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up. Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes. Prop. 43 will restore the two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including any tax increases placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative. It’s a constitutional amendment, overriding court precedents that say otherwise. General taxes, such as those that direct the revenue into a city or county general fund to be spent as elected officials decide, would continue to require only a simple majority vote. Some local government officials may believe voters will not approve general taxes, so they would prefer to tell voters the money from a new tax will be spent only on a specific, urgent need. Their problem isn’t the constitution, it’s trust — if voters don’t trust local elected officials to spend tax money on the most important priorities first, a majority may vote ‘no’ on any tax unless they know what it will fund and it’s guaranteed in writing. Those same officials undoubtedly benefit from having a court-created loophole to raise special taxes without the need for a two-thirds vote. The loophole has been growing with every election. Multiple “citizens’ initiative” tax increases are on the November ballot, racing to squeeze through the opening before voters can hammer boards over it. Prop. 43 gives California voters the opportunity to restore what state courts have eroded: a taxpayer protection in the state constitution that requires local special taxes to have the approval of two-thirds of voters to pass. Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments

By Sandra Lowe, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, a city councilmember from Sonoma believes Proposition 43 enables minority rule, making it harder to fund vital government functions. The opposing view: An anti-tax advocate says Prop. 43 solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied.

Guest Commentary written by

Sometimes things that sound simple are not. 

Let’s take Proposition 43. Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments' decisions: majority rule.  

Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority.

Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected.

In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee.

Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. 

If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote.

The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders.

No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent.

Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions.

The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation.  

Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments

By Sandra Lowe, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, a city councilmember from Sonoma believes Proposition 43 enables minority rule, making it harder to fund vital government functions. The opposing view: An anti-tax advocate says Prop. 43 solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied.

Guest Commentary written by

Sometimes things that sound simple are not. 

Let’s take Proposition 43. Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments' decisions: majority rule.  

Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority.

Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected.

In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee.

Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. 

If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote.

The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders.

No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent.

Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions.

The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation.  

Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime.

Majority rule is the basis of our democracy and a hallmark of a free society. Let's not go backward.
