Why Democrats made a deal
The proposition was the kind of fiscal one-two punch to keep Democrats, local governments and other left-of-center interest groups up at night.
First, it would have limited local transfer taxes — fees on the sale of real estate — to no more than 0.055% (fifty-five cents for every $1,000 in a property’s value). Twenty-six cities, including some of the state’s largest, have levies set well above that cutoff, with Los Angeles’ mansion tax (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), which funds affordable housing and renter assistance, maxing out at 100 times that rate.
The proposition would have also raised the share of votes needed for certain types of local taxes. Though many local tax measures in California require the support of two-thirds of voters, those placed on the ballot through signature gathering campaigns to fund specific purposes only need more than 50% (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/). The Jarvis proposition would have nixed that rule and voided any measures enacted since 2017 that didn’t meet the two-thirds requirement.
Instead, under Thursday’s deal, voters will consider the 50% rule on local tax measures alone, though it would not apply retroactively.
Though public polling (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-education-april-2026/) suggested that Howard Jarvis’s proposition faced long odds in California, lawmakers, unions and other opponents worried that voters could be persuaded to back an anti-tax measure amid heightened concerns about affordability and the cost of living. The double-barrelled tax cut would have blown a multibillion-dollar hole in municipal budgets annually, but would have saved local taxpayers just as much, according to an estimate (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) by the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Cities aren’t enthusiastic about the new deal, which would give voters a chance to cut off what has become a frequently used funding source for public programs.
“At a time when cities are already struggling to maintain a high quality of service in a context of high inflation, runaway costs for basic goods and services, cuts in federal funding, and stagnant sales revenue, efforts that limit the ability to raise local revenues only deepen uncertainty for local governments and the communities they serve,” Carolyn Coleman, director of the League of California Cities, said in a written statement.
Even so, the league said it does not yet have a formal position on the new measure.
The bargain also removed an especially convoluted constitutional amendment (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) from the ballot that was designed to ensnare the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association by requiring any future proposition that wanted to hike the voter threshold needed to pass a law (say, from 50% to two-thirds) to itself pass by the higher threshold.
What about transfer taxes?
Left out of the compromise is anything about transfer taxes, a topic that has dominated the public debate (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) over the proposition and provided much of the fuel for its earlier signature gathering campaign.
On Monday, Wicks, who is aligned with the pro-development “Yes In My Backyard” movement, rolled out Assembly Bill 736 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736) as a possible legislative off-ramp. The bill would have capped transfer taxes at between 1.5% and 3%, depending on the type of tax. That’s well above the Howard Jarvis-backed cut-off, but would have been a significant rate cut for a handful of high-tax municipalities like Los Angeles, Santa Monica, Culver City, San Jose and San Francisco.
For Wicks and her YIMBY allies, the bill is seen as more than a simple electoral instrument. Pro-development groups have pointed to high transfer taxes (https://housingactioncoalition.org/news/hac-ed-homes4good-transfer-tax) as one of many impediments to the construction of much-needed housing.
The proposal also got the backing of the California Business Roundtable, a large business coalition whose members include major real estate investors and which has been bankrolling the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association’s campaign.
With the funders endorsing a legislative compromise, it seemed possible that the taxpayers association would also be willing to back the lower tax cap.
The political pressure ratcheted up even further on Wednesday. As Politico first reported, the heads of three major real estate investment firms said that they were ready to spend at least $10 million (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/06/tax-initiative-funders-flip-ballot-initiative-00975300) battling the measure if Coupal didn’t back down.
Until the final hours, it seemed like he wouldn’t.
“We’ve had lots of partners help us qualify this initiative, but we are the ultimate decider as to whether or not we proceed with our initiative,” said Jon Coupal, the association’s president told CalMatters earlier this week. “It is our intention to proceed.”
Striking a deal that could make it harder to raise new local taxes represents a long-sought policy win (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) for the taxpayer group. Capping transfer taxes appears to have been less of a priority. The Wicks bill “is floating out there which people can support or not support, it’s up to them,” he said.
But the political calculus over AB 736has changed. Even before Thursday’s deal was announced, an ideologically diverse array of interest groups had already rallied to defeat it: The California Association of Realtors, local government groups, many affordable housing developers and tenant rights advocates.
Without a proposition hanging over their head anymore, legislators aren’t likely to have much appetite to take such a difficult vote.
All eyes on LA
The transfer tax omission comes as a disappointment to many real estate interests and pro-development advocates, particularly in Los Angeles, which has been the center of the statewide debate over transfer taxes this year.
Since 2023, the city has had the among the highest transfer taxes in California in the form of Measure ULA. That policy, backed by the city’s voters, places a 4% tax on real estate sales over roughly $5 million and 5.5% on those just above $10 million. So far it’s raised more than $1.2 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) for affordable housing, renter assistance and eviction defense.
But despite the “mansion tax” moniker, the tax also applies to apartment developments, condos, commercial and industrial projects. A number of academic analyses have blamed the tax for the city’s abnormal drop in new multifamily housing construction and for reducing property tax revenue. Politically, the animosity toward Measure ULA by Los Angeles-based real estate developers and investors has provided significant fuel (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/#:~:text=along,ULA) behind the Howard Jarvis measure, the proposition’s backers have said.
“It’s crazy that poorly designed transfer taxes like Measure ULA spurred this effort, but at the end of the day, Measure ULA and other similar measures will remain untouched,” said Mott Smith, chairman of the Council of Infill Builders and prominent advocate for changing the L.A. tax.
Change may still be on the docket for Los Angeles. Earlier this month, the city council voted to put a measure on the local ballot to exempt apartment and mixed-use buildings (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/mansion-tax-housing-ballot-measure-city-council-vote-november) from the higher transfer tax within the 10 years of construction. That proposal is expected to get a final council vote next week.
The failure to address transfer taxes only reinforces the need for Los Angeles to act, said Leo Daube, a spokesperson for Councilmember Katy Yaroslavsky, who introduced the proposed change.
“If Sacramento is not going to do it, then Los Angeles should,” he said.

Bay Area officials are sounding the alarm over a lesser-known California ballot measure
By Kathryn Palmer (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kathryn-palmer/) , Staff Writer Oct 12, 2026
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie appears alongside first responders to oppose Proposition 43 outside of Fire Station No. 5 on Oct. 7.
Weston Turtle Fudge/S.F. Chronicle
It’s not often that the supporters and opponents of a ballot measure agree on what exactly it would do, let alone describe it the same way. Yet both sides of the fight over Proposition 43 have been clear: It will make it harder to raise local taxes.
What they don’t agree on is whether it’s a good idea.
Bay Area leaders last week joined a growing chorus of local government officials across the state voicing strong opposition to Proposition 43, slamming the measure as a threat to critical financial lifelines for cities and counties.

Article continues below this ad
Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday also said he plans to vote against Prop 43, siding with a wide collection of Democratic lawmakers and local government officials who oppose the measure.
Supporters, led by the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, argue that as the state and nation grapple with an affordability crisis, raising taxes should be difficult.
General taxes, which aren’t earmarked for a specific use and go into a city’s general fund, can pass with a simple majority. But taxes that will go toward a specific purpose — like pay raises for police and fire personnel, or homeless services — are subject to a much higher two-thirds vote requirement when they’re placed on the ballot by government officials.
This puts anyone looking to raise revenue in a strange bind: Voters are much more likely to support a tax increase when they know it’s going to fix a specific problem. They’re less likely to OK a general tax hike that could fund virtually anything. Yet the two-thirds requirement is a significant hurdle, making it almost impossible to raise special taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 43 would extend that two-thirds threshold to special tax measures placed on the ballot by citizen initiatives, not just those spearheaded by government officials. It would mean all special taxes would need to be approved by a much higher percentage of voters than other ballot measures.
Local leaders across California, including many in the Bay Area, have begun sounding the alarm over the implications if Prop 43 were to pass.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, and Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee joined San Francisco Supervisor Bilal Mahmood and representatives of housing and public safety groups last week to urge voters to reject the measure, warning it would hamstring communities’ ability to raise funds for local needs. They also warned that it would enhance the veto power of a select few, potentially inviting “special interests” to try to sway election outcomes.
“Prop 43 undermines democracy by upending majority rule, making it harder for communities across California to support first responders, parks, libraries and affordable housing,” Lurie said at a press conference in San Francisco last week. “Voters know what our communities need to keep our neighborhoods safe, keep Muni moving, and build more housing.”
Supporters have cast the court decisions allowing citizens’ special tax initiatives to pass by simple majority as a loophole. If Prop 43 passes, it would essentially hit the rewind button to a period before a 2017 state Supreme Court decision led to the current simple majority rule.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association spokesperson Susan Shelley said local governments would still be able to pass general tax increases by a simple majority under Prop 43, and argued local officials should prioritize their budgets to pay for essential services first.
“Proposition 43 makes it harder to raise taxes, like sales taxes,” Shelley said. “It restores the requirement for a two-thirds vote of the people if the money from a local tax will be earmarked and locked for a special purpose.”
Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee, third from left, appears in San Francisco alongside first responders to oppose Proposition 43.
Weston Turtle Fudge/S.F. Chronicle The ballot measure also counts Reform California as a supporter, the campaign group helmed by firebrand GOP Assembly Member Carl DeMaio.
The California Republican Party, along with some Republican lawmakers and a few current and former Bay Area officials, back the measure. The list includes Debora Allen, former BART director, and Quentin Kopp, former San Francisco supervisor.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The coalition of those fighting Prop 43 got a boost last week when Newsom endorsed a no vote, a position in lockstep with the California Democratic Party, several prominent Democratic state and local lawmakers, and associations representing California cities and counties.
The League of California Cities opposes Prop 43, as does the California State Association of Counties and the California Special Districts Association, collectively representing hundreds of municipalities across the state.
Susan Ellenberg, president of the California State Association of Counties, said in a statement to the Chronicle that many local needs depend on community-driven funding, such as wildfire prevention, emergency response and behavioral health.
“The measure would also limit residents’ ability to propose and approve solutions through the initiative process, even when those solutions earn broad majority support,” said Ellenberg, who is also a Santa Clara County supervisor. “For local governments already facing strained budgets and increasing responsibilities, this change would reshape how communities address their most pressing priorities.”
Ellenberg and other Santa Clara County leaders backed a 2024 tax increase that they billed as a measure to fund healthcare services in the wake of Trump administration cuts. But Measure A was a general tax increase, subject to the much lower vote threshold, meaning the money can technically be spent on anything. It passed with 57% of the vote.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
As of Tuesday, the Yes on 43 campaign has a slight financial edge, banking more than $10 million in campaign funds so far. The anti-43 campaign reported just under $8 million.
In 2024, eight special sales tax measures qualified for local ballots across the state by a citizens initiative, with increases ranging from one-fourth of a cent to 1 cent. Of the four that passed with a simple majority, none met Prop 43’s two-thirds vote threshold. The two that received the most support were Sonoma County’s Measure I to fund childcare and Benicia’s Measure F to fund road improvements. They passed at 62% and 61%, respectively.
Other prominent special tax measures include the Los Angeles mansion tax, which voters passed by majority in 2022 and places a 4% tax on real estate sales on multimillion-dollar homes.
Prop 43 arose out of a deal cut to avoid another qualified ballot measure from the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association that took aim at elements of the mansion tax.
It was that last-minute legislative brokering that led the anti-tax group to instead put forward Prop 43, with the help of Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland. Soon after Prop 43 qualified for the November ballot, Wicks disavowed it, calling it “the only path left to get the more dangerous initiative off the ballot.”
Isaac Martin, a sociology professor at UC San Diego who has written multiple books about taxation and public finance, described Prop 43 as affecting a Goldilocks-like subset of tax measures: popular enough for a simple majority, but not popular enough to pass overwhelmingly.
“Since it would make it harder for local governments to raise money for popular services, the options are to raise funds for general government, including popular and less popular services, or do without,” Martin said. “I mean, bottom line, those are sort of the only options for local governments.”
Groups that oppose the measure argue the new threshold would make it harder for communities to make hyper-specific funding decisions to tackle local priorities.
Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters advocacy group representing thousands of firefighters, said the measure risks cutting off crucial public safety funding. He pointed to Measure H in Sonoma County and Measure E in Los Angeles County, both passed by voters in 2024. Both taxes raise funds to bolster the two counties’ fire protection and emergency response services — top priorities in regions that have been devastated by some of the state’s deadliest wildfires in recent years.
“Any time you have local elected leaders, public safety and community advocates, or people that are running local health clinics or infrastructure projects, say that they need to get something done in their community, it should be the community that decides, with a simple majority,” Roberts said.

PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 43
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43: THE LOCAL TAXPAYER PROTECTION ACT
California families are struggling with the highest income, sales, and gas taxes in the nation. Yet politicians and special interests keep pushing higher taxes that make our cost of living even more expensive.
We can’t afford to pay ANY MORE in new or higher taxes. PROP. 43 RESTORES PROPOSITION 13 TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
Proposition 13 was designed to make it harder to raise taxes, but court decisions created loopholes that allow special interests to impose massive new tax increases by circumventing the taxpayer protections voters approved. Californians are paying billions in new or higher taxes they would not have to pay if it weren’t for these loopholes. Prop. 43 closes these loopholes and restores the two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO RAISE YOUR TAXES
Local governments have imposed over 2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade, including higher sales, property and utility taxes-using the loopholes courts created in Prop. 13 to impose some of the most costly and damaging tax increases Californians face today.
These new and higher taxes make everything we buy or use more expensive, from food and gas to utilities and housing.
Prop. 43 guarantees voters the right to vote on all local taxes and restores the two-thirds vote for special local taxes.
PROP. 43 PROTECTS HOMEOWNERS FROM COSTLY NEW REAL ESTATE TAXES
California already has some of the highest housing costs in America, yet special interests are using court-created loopholes to add new taxes on the sale of homes, apartments and other real estate.
Some cities now charge real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%. For California’s median-priced home of $900,000, that would cost a homeowner $54,000 simply for selling their house. Those costs steal homeowners’ equity, raise apartment rents, and make building new housing more expensive.
Prop. 43 makes it much harder for special interests to impose these costly taxes on homeowners, renters, and small businesses.
PROP. 43 STOPS THE BAIT-AND-SWITCH TAX TRICKS
Politicians and special interests promise new taxes will fund schools, roads, and public safety-only to divert the money elsewhere and frustrate the will of voters. Prop. 43 requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved and restores the broad voter support required before politicians and special interests impose earmarked tax measures.
If taxpayers are asked to pay more, they deserve the right to vote and the confidence their money will be spent as promised.
PROP. 43 PUTS VOTERS BACK IN CHARGE
Every election, politicians say they need just one more tax increase. Prop. 43 simply ensures TAXPAYERS are fully protected by the right to vote on taxes.
Vote YES on Prop. 43:
• Affirms the voters’ right to vote on all new or higher local taxes. • Restores the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. • Protects Proposition 13 and closes court-created loopholes. • Makes it harder for special interests to raise taxes. • Protects homeowners, renters, and small businesses from new real estate taxes. • Strengthens accountability for how taxpayer dollars are spent.
Robert Gutierrez , President
California Taxpayers Association
Robert Rivinius , President
Family Business Association of California
Julian Canete , President
California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 43
We all want relief from California’s high cost of living. But Proposition 43 doesn’t cut your taxes a penny. It attacks something far more valuable: the power of your vote.
PROP. 43 WEAKENS YOUR VOTE.
Today, when local voters decide how to fund their communities, the majority rules. Prop. 43 throws that out, letting just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Under Prop. 43, a NO vote counts twice as much as a YES. That isn’t fair, and it isn’t democracy.
PROP. 43 DEEPENS THE HOUSING CRISIS.
Across California, communities vote to build affordable homes for working families, seniors, and veterans. They are helping renters stay housed and move people off the streets. Prop. 43 hands a small minority the power to block those solutions, even when a clear majority of your neighbors support them.
PROP. 43 TIES YOUR COMMUNITY’S HANDS.
Prop. 43 makes it harder for you to fund the critical local services your community counts on: staffing fire stations and 911 response, preparing neighborhoods for wildfire, repairing crumbling roads, keeping schools, parks, and libraries open, and protecting local hospitals and clinics as Washington cuts healthcare funding. When funding is blocked, help arrives slower, classrooms grow more crowded, and communities are left less safe.
KEEP THE POWER WHERE IT BELONGS-WITH YOU AND YOUR NEIGHBORS.
That’s why teachers, nurses, firefighters, and housing advocates all oppose Prop. 43.
VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION 43.
www.NoProp43CA.com
Nick Lapis , Director of Advocacy
Californians Against Waste
Bill Barnes , Director of Campaigns & Community
Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California
Steve Frisch , President
Sierra Business Council
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 43
PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES.
Prop. 43 makes it harder for you to fund critical services like police and fire departments, fix and repair local roads, staff our local schools or backfill federal healthcare cuts. Prop. 43 undermines the voice of voters and the majority vote by letting just one-third of voters (33.4%) block local voter decisions-and it makes it easier for corporate special interests to avoid paying their fair share.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO FUND FIRE AND POLICE SERVICES.
Local police and firefighters can’t rely on Sacramento or Washington politicians. These services are funded at the local level. Prop. 43 wants to make it harder for local voters to direct new funding to services like police and fire. Without adequate funding, 911 response times are slower, fire stations sit understaffed, and families wait longer for help when every second counts. When a house fire breaks out-or a wildfire threatens our neighborhoods-that local funding is what protects us. Prop. 43 would let a small minority of voters block it. Even if 66% of voters say yes, Prop. 43 would prevent us from funding desperately needed local services.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO FIX ROADS, FUND SCHOOLS, AND PROTECT HEALTHCARE.
Across California, local voters have come together to repair crumbling roads and improve transportation, to fund their neighborhood schools, and to protect local hospitals and healthcare-especially as Washington cuts federal health funding. These are decisions communities make for themselves, by majority vote. Instead, Prop. 43 hands a small group of voters the power to veto those solutions, even when the majority supports them.
PROP. 43 EMPOWERS 33.4% OF VOTERS OVER THE WILL OF THE MAJORITY.
In America, we believe in one person, one vote-and the majority wins. Prop. 43 throws that out. It empowers just over one-third of voters to block what nearly 67% want. It puts the out-voted minority in charge-even if they are extremists. It makes their NO vote count twice as much as a YES vote.
CORPORATE DONORS BENEFIT. NOT TAXPAYERS.
Under Prop. 43, corporate donors who spend big in elections will benefit most. Right now, voters can hold these corporations and developers accountable at the ballot box, and make them pay their fair share for local needs. Prop. 43 is designed to take that power away-to protect the powerful few, at everyone else’s expense.
That’s why these organizations are asking you to vote NO on Prop. 43:
• California Professional Firefighters • Californians Against Waste • California Federation of Teachers • California School Employees Association • Communities for a Better Environment • AAPI Force • Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California • Nurses Alliance of SEIU California • Sierra Business Council
Vote NO to protect your vote and majority rule. Keep the power where it belongs-with you and your neighbors.
VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION 43.
www.NoProp43CA.com
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Chris Harkins , Executive Director
Nurse Alliance of SEIU California
Adam Weinberger , President

REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 43
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43 TO RESTORE TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
Californians already pay high taxes. But instead of prioritizing funding for critical services like police and fire, local politicians waste your money on their pet projects- then demand tax increases, claiming the need to fund the most important priorities.
The state Constitution requires a two-thirds vote for taxes earmarked for a specific purpose, but recent court decisions created a loophole that allowed special taxes to pass with fewer votes. Now Californians are paying billions in taxes they should not have had to pay.
Prop. 43 RESTORES the longstanding two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes, protecting homeowners, renters, and small businesses from costly new sales and parcel taxes, taxes on electricity and gas, and real estate taxes.
Prop. 43 GUARANTEES taxpayers the right to vote on new or higher local taxes and requires governments to spend taxpayer dollars for the specific purposes voters approved-preventing bait-and-switch schemes that make our sky-high cost of living even worse.
Over the last decade, local governments have imposed 2,000 new or higher taxes. Prop. 43 CLOSES LOOPHOLES used to pass some of the most damaging tax increases, restores the protections voters originally approved under Proposition 13, and makes it harder for special interests to raise taxes without broad voter support.
The Legislature’s nearly unanimous vote to place Prop. 43 on the ballot sends a clear message: activist courts exceeded voters’ intent by creating loopholes that weakened Proposition 13’s protections.
Restore your right to vote on ALL local taxes.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43

Now let me consider the analysis and form a recommendation.

Key facts:
- Prop 43 (ACA 22, Wicks) adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A: beginning Jan 1, 2027, no local government, including the electorate exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax unless approved by two-thirds vote. Also bars ad valorem property taxes by initiative.
- Currently, citizen-initiated special taxes pass with simple majority (per Upland 2017 and subsequent appellate rulings, which the CA Supreme Court effectively affirmed in the Prop C litigation).
- Prospective only; doesn't undo existing taxes.
- Support: HJTA, CalTax, Reform California, CA Republican Party, small business groups. Raised ~$14.9M (Sept 19) / $10M+ by October.
- Oppose: CA Democratic Party, Newsom, author Wicks, League of Women Voters, firefighters, teachers, nurses, SEIU, counties association, League of California Cities, special districts association, mayors of SF and Oakland, Evolve California, CalBudgetCenter. Raised ~$4.9M (Sept) / ~$8M by October.
- Polls: PPIC 42-55 no; IGS 36-46 no. Likely to fail but within reach given undecideds.
- SF Chronicle editorial board: neither supports nor opposes (says it "further cements a broken system" but won't oppose; argues if it passes maybe it'll force comprehensive tax reform). LA Times (Skelton): No.
- LWVC: No.
- Notable: some progressive/YIMBY arguments in favor: citizen-initiative special taxes have been used to enact bad policy (LA Measure ULA at 58%, SF Prop C at 61% — a business tax; SF's Prop I 2026 which the Chronicle calls "horrible policy"). The two-thirds threshold for government-proposed special taxes has been in place since 1978 and California has functioned.

Now, what should the user vote? Let me think about the substantive merits carefully.

Arguments for YES:
1. Consistency: A special tax is a special tax regardless of who puts it on the ballot. The current double standard (government-proposed special taxes need 2/3; citizen-initiated need only majority) is a procedural anomaly created by court interpretation, and it incentivizes gaming — local officials route taxes through citizen committees to avoid the higher threshold. Indeed, that's a well-documented practice: many "citizen initiatives" are actually government-backed measures placed through signature gathering by supporters precisely to get the lower threshold. E.g., LA County Measure A? Actually the Chronicle said Measure A was a general tax. But there are numerous examples where city councils deliberately declined to place a measure and let citizens do it to get majority threshold. This is real "ballot engineering."
2. Supermajority requirements for earmarked taxes have deep roots in CA law (Prop 13, 218) and reflect a broad consensus that dedicating revenue to specific purposes (which reduces budget flexibility and creates ratchet effects) should require wide support.
3. It doesn't ban anything; general taxes still pass by majority. Local governments retain the majority-vote path.
4. Fiscal discipline / affordability: California has among the highest combined state+local tax burdens and cost of living; raising the bar for earmarked tax increases is defensible.
5. Some citizen-initiative special taxes have been harmful (LA Measure ULA — documented decline in multifamily construction and revenue; SF Prop C gross receipts tax on large businesses).
6. The measure is prospective only and narrow — the more damaging retroactive initiative was withdrawn. So a Yes vote here locks in a modest, clear rule and possibly discourages future sweeping attacks (though that's speculative).

Arguments for NO:
1. Supermajority requirements are anti-majoritarian: 33.4% can block 66.6%. Especially pernicious because a "no" vote effectively counts double.
2. It specifically burdens the citizen initiative — the core tool of direct democracy designed for when elected officials won't act. Asymmetry: it doesn't restrict the government-proposed path (already 2/3) — so effectively, it only takes away a power voters currently have. That's a net reduction in popular sovereignty.
3. Empirically, several measures that funded fire protection, childcare, roads, homelessness, and healthcare passed with majority but not 2/3 support — e.g., Sonoma County Measure I (childcare, 62%), Benicia Measure F (roads, 61%), LA Measure ULA (58%), SF Prop C (61%), Fresno Measure P (52%), Madera Measure T (52%), Sonoma County Measure H and LA County Measure E (2024 fire protection). 4. Context: local governments face federal funding cuts (H.R. 1 Medi-Cal/CalFresh cuts), wildfire costs, inflation, and are already constrained by Prop 13's property tax cap and Prop 218's limits on fees/assessments. Adding another constraint reduces capacity to fund services, likely increasing reliance on state funds (more volatile) and regressive fees.
5. The measure was a backroom deal — the author herself opposes it, and the Legislature passed it 68-2 / 35-1 largely as a hostage-trade to kill a worse initiative. That's a poor basis for constitutional amendment.
6. The official title, written by the AG/Legislature, is itself negative: "Limits voters' ability to raise revenues for local government services."
7. It would entrench a two-tier system where organized, well-funded "no" campaigns (which are cheaper to run — just block) can veto. Given that supermajority thresholds systematically favor status quo/wealthy interests.
8. Counterargument to "consistency": If you're worried about consistency, the better fix is to lower the threshold for all local special taxes to a majority (as Prop 5 in 2024 tried for bonds and lost) rather than raise the citizen path to 2/3. Raising the bar for the only majority-vote path is a ratchet against democracy.

Supermajority requirements for taxation are a minority veto; the measure uniquely targets the one path where the electorate itself acts, and its practical effect is to make it harder for communities to fund services during a period of federal cuts. # 2026 California Proposition 43
**Proposition 43** is a proposed legislative constitutional amendment on the November 3, 2026, ballot in California.
Starting on January 1, 2027, Proposition 43 would restore the two-thirds voter approval requirement to impose, extend, or increase a local special (legally dedicated) tax under Proposition 13 for any proposed special tax that qualifies for the ballot under the local initiative power.^[1]^ Proposition 43 would also prohibit local governments, including under the local initiative power, from imposing additional ad valorem taxes on real property (taxes based on the assessed value of property), except as otherwise allowed under the California Constitution.^[2]^
Proposition 43 was proposed to overturn appellate court rulings following the 2017 *Upland* decision by the California Supreme Court,^[3]^ which created a distinction between taxes proposed by the governing body of a local government and taxes proposed under the local initiative power for purposes of applying the two-thirds voter approval requirement for special taxes under Proposition 13.
These appellate court rulings held that citizen-led special tax proposals under the local initiative power were no longer subject to the two-thirds voter approval requirement under Proposition 13.

Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives and Property Tax Initiative Prohibition Amendment
Summary
Placed on the ballot via 2025-2026 Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22 (ACA 22 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) ), Proposition 43 proposes adding Section 4.5 to Article XII of the California Constitution. The measure increases the approval threshold for citizen-initiated local special tax measures, requiring a two-thirds (66.67%) vote to enact, extend, or raise special taxes at the local level.
F iscal Impact
There is a possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes.
What your vote means
YES: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
NO: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 43 protects taxpayers by requiring a two-thirds voter majority for local special tax increases, closing legal loopholes that previously allowed them to pass with a simple majority.
Opponents contend that this higher voting threshold allows a minority of voters to block popular measures, making it much harder for local communities to fund essential public services like schools, roads, and emergency response. Ultimately, the measure pits stronger taxpayer protections against the ability of local communities to raise funding by majority rule.

Proposition 43
Raise vote threshold for special tax measures
This would make it harder to impose or increase local taxes by raising the threshold for local citizen-driven special tax ballot initiatives to pass from a simple majority to two-thirds. The two-thirds threshold already applies to taxes proposed by local governments but not by individuals. The measure reflects a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.

All the tax measures on the LA, OC ballots
Erin Rode (https://laist.com/people/erin-rode)
is working on election coverage this fall, along with other topics.
Published October 28, 2026 4:00 PM
More than 30 cities in L.A. and Orange counties have tax increases of some kind on the Nov. 3 ballot.
( Raymond Rivera
/
For LAist
)
Topline:
By LAist’s count, over 30 cities in Los Angeles and Orange counties are asking residents to approve tax measures on Election Day this Tuesday.
Why now? Municipalities cite stagnant revenues that haven’t kept pace with the rising costs of insurance, maintenance and infrastructure projects, and employee pensions. As a result, big cities, suburbs and small towns alike are all facing multimillion-dollar budget deficits. So they are asking residents to open their wallets — or potentially see deep cuts to basic city services.
Read on ... to find out if possible hikes are coming your way.
Full Story
Southern Californians are feeling squeezed by the rising costs of, well, everything. And now their local governments are asking for more money, too.
By LAist’s count, more than 30 cities or districts in Los Angeles and Orange counties are asking residents to approve tax measures on Election Day, Nov. 3, citing stagnant revenues that haven’t kept pace with the rising costs of insurance, maintenance and infrastructure projects, and employee pensions. Big cities, suburbs and small towns are all facing multimillion-dollar budget deficits and asking residents to open their wallets — or potentially see deep cuts to basic city services.
The list of local measures on ballots from Culver City to San Clemente includes sales taxes, hotel taxes, business taxes, parcel taxes and utility taxes. Some ballot measures would extend or increase existing taxes while others are brand-new.
Much of the answer to why so many tax measures are on the ballot lies in Proposition 13, which capped property taxes in 1978.
Before Prop. 13, cities and counties relied on property taxes for nearly all of their revenue. In the decades since, they’ve increasingly turned to other types of taxes. Hotel and utility taxes, for example, were essentially nonexistent (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497#How_Did_Proposition.A013_Change_Local_Governments_Mix_of_Tax_Revenues.3F) before the mid-1970s, and sales taxes represented a small sliver of revenue. Even as these taxes have grown, they’ve struggled to replace property tax revenue.
How Proposition 13 reshaped local taxes
Before 1978, California municipalities could raise taxes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx) without voter approval. But in addition to capping property taxes, Proposition 13 also changed the rules for other taxes. Section 4 of Proposition 13 states that any special taxes (which are taxes designated for a specific use) must be approved by two-thirds of voters. A later proposition passed in 1986 (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx) requires that general taxes be approved by a simple majority of voters. General taxes are general purpose funds that cities can allocate as they please.
The rules could change again this year with Proposition 43 (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-43-local-special-tax), which would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens to two-thirds. Currently, citizen-led special tax initiatives only need to win a simple majority.
Despite what the Nov. 3 ballot might suggest, sales tax measures are actually becoming less common, according to Michael Coleman, author of the California Local Government Finance Almanac (https://www.californiacityfinance.com/#VOTES). “More and more governments have started to exhaust the capacity for that. There’s a limit in how much you can do both legally and in terms of the tolerance of voters,” Coleman said. State law caps the maximum combined local and county sales tax rate, and many Southern California cities are already at or near that cap, Coleman said. And sales tax isn’t as reliable as it used to be, amid the broader retail downturn and shift to a service-based economy (most services aren’t taxable in California).
All of that means cities are increasingly turning to “ticky-tacky, peculiar taxes” to come up with revenue, according to Kirk Stark, a professor of tax law and policy at UCLA.
The “conventional tax instruments” — property, income and sales taxes — are all limited by state law, Stark said. “Local governments that are hoping to satisfy demand for any kind of public expenditure have to turn to other, less conventional sources of revenue.”
This year, cities are asking Southern Californians to say yes to a wide range of taxes. Below, we look at three examples in South Gate, Orange and Diamond Bar.
South Gate: A utility users tax
South Gate is asking voters to approve something less common: a utility users tax, or UUT for short. If Measure SG is approved, the 8% tax would be added to bills for utilities (https://www.cityofsouthgate.org/files/sharedassets/public/v/2/government/departments/administrative-services/budgets-amp-financial-transparency/documents/item-no.-2-uut-understanding-fiscal-challenge-presentation-4.20.26-website.pdf) such as electricity, water, natural gas, cable and phone service. The tax would bring in an estimated $10.4 million (https://www.cityofsouthgate.org/files/sharedassets/public/v/1/government/city-manager/documents/uut/sg-water-bills-insert-measure-sg.pdf) per year.
The city is facing a potential fiscal emergency and a $9.4 million budget deficit. Earlier this year, South Gate began cutting back services, including eliminating its crossing guard program and assigning fewer police officers per shift.
At a City Council meeting (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uDUbDpm7wIU&t=6192s) on the tax measure earlier this year, several residents spoke against the measure, with some calling the deficit a result of potential financial mismanagement that shouldn’t be pushed onto residents. Others said the monthly costs would simply add a new burden to already tight budgets.
“Being a homeowner here for the past 13 years, I have seen my utilities go up as well as the cost of living, my insurance for my house, and my car insurance go up. I believe there’s got to be a way to fix this problem without the UUT measure,” one resident told the City Council.
“I’m extremely frustrated that you now want to do electricity, water, sewer, cable, cell phone, gas. ... That hurts us. You’re passing that on to us, and that is absolutely not acceptable,” said another.
The only other utility users tax on the ballot in Los Angeles or Orange counties this year is in San Marino, where residents will decide whether to extend the city’s existing 5% utility users tax, which is set to expire on March 31, 2027 (https://sanmarinoca.gov/government/elections/utility_users_tax_information.php), and increase it to 6%. Last year, the tax provided almost $2.2 million (https://cms9files.revize.com/cityofsanmarino/City%20Clerk/elections/StaffReport_CONSIDERATION%20OF%20RESOLUTION%20NO.%20R-26-28.pdf?t=202607291247200) in revenue. As of 2021, a total of 162 out of 540 California cities and counties (https://californiacityfinance.com/UUTfacts21.pdf) had a utility users tax, according to Coleman’s California Local Government Finance Almanac (https://californiacityfinance.com/UUTfacts21.pdf).
Orange: Hotel and sales taxes could go up
Most people don’t book a hotel in their own city. That’s made hotel taxes an easier pill to swallow (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx) for voters, since the tax is mostly levied on visitors.
The city of Orange is asking voters to approve Measure J, which would raise the hotel tax (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/J-ORAN%20TOT%20-%20LAYOUT%20(1).pdf) from 10% to 14%. Orange is one of 10 cities across Los Angeles and Orange counties where voters will decide in November whether to increase or establish a local hotel tax, also known as a “transient occupancy tax.”
Orange residents will also vote on a 1-cent sales tax measure (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/I-ORAN%20Sales%20Tax%20-%20LAYOUT%20(1).pdf), as the city projects a $27.6 million deficit that it calls (https://www.cityoforange.org/our-city/revenue-measures) “one of the largest financial challenges in the city’s history.” The sales tax is expected to bring in $37 million annually (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/I-ORAN%20Sales%20Tax%20-%20LAYOUT%20%281%29.pdf), and the hotel tax would add $3 million (https://ocvote.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/J-ORAN%20TOT%20-%20LAYOUT%20(1).pdf).
Diamond Bar: A new 1-cent sales tax
Diamond Bar voters will decide on Measure Q, a 1% local sales tax that would add a penny per dollar to purchases of taxable items. The city estimates the tax will bring in an additional $6 million annually, which could help plug a projected budget deficit of $5 million a year by 2030.
“The city’s challenge is simple: costs for city services are going up faster than revenues,” states Diamond Bar’s fact sheet (https://www.diamondbarca.gov/1309/Measure-Q-Preserving-Diamond-Bars-Qualit#docaccess-5e868454e42f489f95eaa188c3a27550) on the measure, which cites rising public safety costs and $100 million in infrastructure and maintenance needs.
Several other cities have local sales tax measures on the ballot, including Santa Ana’s 1.5% sales tax (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-orange-county-general-santa-ana-measure-n) extension and Los Angeles’ sales tax (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-general-los-angeles-measure-fd-sales-tax) increase for the Los Angeles Fire Department, Measure FD.
“There’s a variety because circumstances among these local governments vary. The types of economies among governments vary, the local conditions, even the preferences for what type of revenue measure or tax measure might work varies,” Coleman said. “A local government that’s looking at one of these is going to look at a number of different options and consider what might be most palatable to the voters in their community.”
What’s on your ballot?
Our LAist Voter Game Plan is here to help guide you through the Nov. 3 election with guides to races across Los Angeles and Orange counties — and that long list of state propositions — to help you cast a ballot that’s in line with your own personal beliefs and values.
But the one thing we don’t do? We don’t tell you how to vote. That part is left up to you.
You can find it all at LAist.com/Vote (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides).

Below, an anti-tax advocate says Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied. Guest Commentary written by Susan Shelley Susan Shelley is the vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The November ballot measure Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) would make it harder to raise taxes in California by restoring the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. A “special tax” is one that earmarks the revenue for specific purposes. Ever since voters approved Proposition 13 in 1978 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)), the California Constitution has clearly stated that cities, counties and special districts may impose special taxes “by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district.” If courts had enforced that plain language, Californians today would not be paying billions of dollars in local taxes. This includes sales tax increases such as L.A. County’s 2024 Measure A (https://homeless.lacounty.gov/measure-a/) for homelessness programs, as well as Measure ULA in the city of Los Angeles (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/), a real estate transfer tax on the value of a property worth more than $5 million, which also pays for homelessness programs and affordable housing. Neither of these received the constitutionally required 66.67% of the vote. In San Francisco, courts upheld a June 2018 special tax (http://sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-appeals-court-upholds-S-F-s-commercial-15903302.php) on commercial real estate leases to fund early education and child care, and a November 2018 special tax on the gross receipts of businesses to pay for homelessness programs. Just like Los Angeles, these measures fell short of a two-thirds vote. In 1978, the people of California added the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes to their constitution. When did the constitution become merely advisory? READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/) It began in 2017 with ambiguous language in a California Supreme Court decision, California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (https://cases.justia.com/california/supreme-court/2017-s234148.pdf?ts=1503939675) . The court suggested — without really deciding — that if a tax increase was placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative instead of by a city council or other government body, the constitution didn’t necessarily apply, and a two-thirds vote wasn’t necessarily required. Lower courts used that language to uphold special taxes that received less than a two-thirds vote if they were placed on the ballot by voters signing initiative petitions. But who are these citizens who want to stand outside grocery stores and farmer’s markets with clipboards to raise their own taxes? They’re often the people who will get the money from the tax. The Upland decision has essentially enabled special interest groups (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) to write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves, pay to collect the signatures to get it on the ballot, and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Some of the court rulings on these Upland taxes have even allowed local government officials to work hand-in-glove with special interests (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/the-fiction-of-citizens-tax-initiatives-in-california/) to get tax increases on the ballot as “citizens’ initiatives.” Now the state government is pushing the envelope even further. The governor recently signed Assembly Bill 1923 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1923), requiring the Fresno County Registrar of Voters to place a citizens’ initiative sales tax increase for transportation on the November ballot (https://fresnoland.org/2026/08/06/better-roads/). The state did this over the objections of the Fresno County Board of Supervisors after it lawfully exercised its discretion under the elections code to order a study of the measure, which would have delayed it past the 2026 ballot deadline and placed it on the 2028 ballot. This is no way to run a railroad. There is no “citizens’ initiative tax increase exception” from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up. Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes. Prop. 43 will restore the two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including any tax increases placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative. It’s a constitutional amendment, overriding court precedents that say otherwise. General taxes, such as those that direct the revenue into a city or county general fund to be spent as elected officials decide, would continue to require only a simple majority vote. Some local government officials may believe voters will not approve general taxes, so they would prefer to tell voters the money from a new tax will be spent only on a specific, urgent need. Their problem isn’t the constitution, it’s trust — if voters don’t trust local elected officials to spend tax money on the most important priorities first, a majority may vote ‘no’ on any tax unless they know what it will fund and it’s guaranteed in writing. Those same officials undoubtedly benefit from having a court-created loophole to raise special taxes without the need for a two-thirds vote. The loophole has been growing with every election. Multiple “citizens’ initiative” tax increases are on the November ballot, racing to squeeze through the opening before voters can hammer boards over it. Prop. 43 gives California voters the opportunity to restore what state courts have eroded: a taxpayer protection in the state constitution that requires local special taxes to have the approval of two-thirds of voters to pass. Guest Commentary written by Sandra Lowe Sandra Lowe is a member of the Sonoma City Council and a longtime political consultant. Sometimes things that sound simple are not. Let’s take Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/). Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments’ decisions: majority rule. Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority. Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected. In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H (https://sonomacounty.gov/administrative-support-and-fiscal-services/county-executives-office/strategic-initiatives/fire-services-project/measure-h) in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee. Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote (https://ballotpedia.org/Sonoma_County,_California,_Measure_H,_Fire_Prevention_and_Disaster_Response_Sales_Tax_Measure_(March_2024)). Proposition 43 cleans up their mistake (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders. No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent. Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions. The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding (https://health.alamedacountyca.gov/program/measures-a-c-and-w/) and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation (https://www.openspaceauthority.org/whats-new/press-release-measure-d). Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime. California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. The opposing view: An anti-tax advocate says Prop. 43 solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied.

Guest Commentary written by

Sometimes things that sound simple are not. 

Let’s take Proposition 43. Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments' decisions: majority rule.  

Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority.

Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected.

In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee.

Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. 

If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote.

The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders.

No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent.

Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions.

The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation.  

Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime.

Majority rule is the basis of our democracy and a hallmark of a free society. Let's not go backward.

I now have a comprehensive picture. Let me consider one more thing: whether local governments themselves frequently route measures through citizen initiatives as a workaround ("the fiction of citizens' tax initiatives in California" — HJTA article). This is a real concern: many "citizen initiatives" are actually orchestrated by city councils/county boards to dodge the 2/3 threshold. That's a genuine governance problem, and Prop 43 would eliminate that gaming. But note that the same problem exists with government-proposed special taxes (2/3 required) — the workaround was invented because the 2/3 requirement is so high. So eliminating the workaround makes the 2/3 requirement truly binding for all earmarked taxes.

Hmm. Let me weigh both sides once more.

Key considerations on the merits:

For YES:
- Restores consistency and closes what is arguably a genuine loophole exploited by both special interests AND local officials.
- Supermajority requirements for earmarked/dedicated taxes are long-standing California policy, reflecting that dedicated taxes reduce fiscal flexibility.
- Prospective only, narrow; the more damaging retroactive/transfer-tax-cap initiative was withdrawn because of this deal.
- California's affordability crisis; local taxes have proliferated (2,000+ new/increased local taxes in a decade).
- Backed by Mercury News, San Diego U-T, Southern California News Group editorial boards; CA Chamber of Commerce.

For NO:
- Anti-democratic: gives a 34% minority a veto, effectively double-weighting "no" votes.
- Uniquely restricts the citizen initiative — the one tool for voters when elected officials won't act. Asymmetric: doesn't lower anything, only removes a power voters currently hold.
- Real-world harm documented: Sonoma County Measure H (fire/emergency services, 62%), LA County Measure A (homelessness, ~57%), Alameda County health care measure, Santa Clara open space Measure D, Benicia roads (61%), Sonoma childcare (62%), LA Measure ULA (58%), Fresno parks (52%), Madera transportation (52%). Under Prop 43, none would have passed.
- Timing is bad: federal H.R. 1 cuts to Medi-Cal/CalFresh shift costs to counties; wildfire/climate costs rising; local revenues stagnant; Prop 13 + Prop 218 already severely limit local revenue options.
- Perverse incentive: pushes local revenue into general taxes (less transparent, no accountability for use) or into fees/assessments that don't require a supermajority and are more regressive. Reduces transparency, doesn't reduce total burden.
- The measure was a backroom political deal; the author opposes it; the Legislature's near-unanimous vote reflected hostage-taking (to remove a worse initiative), not endorsement of the policy.
- Ballot title itself: "Limits voters' ability to raise revenues for local government services."
- Opposed by League of Women Voters, CA Democratic Party, Newsom, firefighters, teachers, nurses, county supervisors association, League of California Cities, special districts association, SF and Oakland mayors, LA Times columnist, Sacramento Bee.
- If consistency is the goal, the democratic fix is to lower thresholds (e.g., to 55% for all local special taxes), not raise the only majority-vote path. Voters rejected Prop 5 (2024) which would have lowered the bond threshold to 55% — but that's a different measure and it was heavily attacked as a realtor giveaway.
- No evidence that supermajority requirements improve service outcomes; the LAO says revenue could be lower, and the Chronicle's own point about Oakland balancing its budget without Measure E shows both cuts and coping are possible.

Counter to the "special interest loophole" argument: Under a supermajority rule, it's the "no" side that benefits from money — blocking is cheaper than persuading. So Prop 43 arguably empowers well-funded corporate/property-owner interests to veto taxes on themselves (which is exactly what happened with ULA). The "no" argument explicitly says "corporate donors benefit." That's a real asymmetry: supermajority thresholds systematically favor entrenched, well-resourced minorities.

Also: is it true that citizen initiatives are frequently fake? HJTA says yes. Some are genuinely government-orchestrated. But many are genuine grassroots (firefighters, childcare advocates, open space). And notably, the government-orchestrated ones exist precisely because the 2/3 threshold makes honest government-sponsored earmarked taxes nearly impossible.

On balance, I think the stronger case is NO. The measure:
(1) reduces democratic power asymmetrically — it only takes away from voters,
(2) has demonstrable real-world costs for public safety, health, housing, and wildfire preparedness in communities that voted for those taxes by clear majorities,
(3) arrives at the worst possible fiscal moment (federal cuts to Medi-Cal/CalFresh, wildfire costs),
(4) doesn't actually lower taxes — it just shifts revenue to less transparent, more regressive channels,
(5) entrenches a supermajority veto that favors well-funded opponents of taxation.

The strongest pro argument (consistency/anti-loophole) is real but is outweighed: consistency could be achieved by lowering, not raising; and a "loophole" that lets a majority of voters fund fire protection is not the kind of abuse the two-thirds rule was meant to prevent.

Also worth noting: it's a constitutional amendment — permanent and hard to reverse (requires another statewide vote). That raises the stakes of an unclear, deal-driven measure with an unnoticed second provision (ad valorem property tax ban by initiative).

I'll vote NO.
